newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria army threatens tough action to end clashes.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria army threatens tough action to end clashes.

text.p: Nigeria's military authorities have said they will no longer tolerate tribal violence threatening the nation's vital oil industry and will take stern measures to restore order.

"We have had enough of this," Major-General Felix Mujakperuo, commander of the 82nd Division of the army, said in the midwestern oil city of Warri at the weekend while touring the area where troops were deployed to end fighting that has claimed many lives and halted some oil production.
The semi-official Daily Times quoted Mujakperuo as saying during his inspection of damaged public facilities and burnt houses that those responsible would be arrested and brought to book.
"(Mujakperuo) went there to assess the situation on ground and take the necessary action," defence headquarters spokesman Colonel Godwin Ugbo told Reuters in Lagos on Monday.
"We want normal activities to resume and it was important for him to go there to see things for himself," he added.
Mujakperuo, a member of Nigeria's Provisional Ruling Council, is based in the eastern city of Enugu but his command extends to Warri, Nigeria's second most important oil city.

Oil accounts for more than 90 percent of Nigeria's foreign exchange income. Last week the army sent troops into Warri to stop month-old fighting by militant youths over the relocation of a local council headquarters from a town of the Ijaw tribe to an Itsekiri settlement.
The defence headquarters spokesman said there had been no clashes between the troops and the youths so far.
"There is no report of new hostility," he added.
The fighting forced Royal Dutch Shell Group Nigerian unit, the biggest oil operator in the West African nation, to suspend some of its production over the weekend.

A senior official of the company in Warri said on Monday that following an agreement reached with the local community on Sunday night, Shell was poised to reopen flow stations whose closure forced it to declare that there would be delays to shipments of its Forcados blend of crude oil.
"We got an agreement with the people last night and we are in the process of reopening two to three flow stations in Ogidigben closed at the weekend," said the Shell official.
Restive tribes in Nigeria's oil-producing swamps frequently vent their anger on Shell to attract the attention of the military government.
